clues.title: Sign: Maximum sign
text: Canadian speed limit signs have the word "Maximum," while U.S. signs use "Speed Limit."

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Checkboard sign
text: This diamond-shaped T-intersection "checkboard" sign is unique to Canada.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Quebec stop sign
text: Stop signs with the word ‘Arret’ are unique to Quebec in Canada.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Saskatchewan alternating insulators
text: Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.
NOTE: This can rarely be seen in Manitoba.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Ontario speed signs
text: Ontario speed limit signs may feature a black section at the bottom, with the words "km/h" or "begins" written in white.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Ontario guard rails
text: In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Ontario diamonds
text: You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Quebec double sign post
text: Double sign posts on warning sings in Canada is unique to Quebec.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Quebec rectangle markers
text: You can find these rectangular markers on the sides of the roads in Québec. The colours can vary.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Quebec guardrail bollards
text: Quebec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Quebec pole stickers
text: Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Manitoba stop signs
text: You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Alberta bollard
text: Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Sask white dashes between lines
text: Those white dashes between yellow lines are most commonly found in Saskatchewan. You can also sometimes find them in BC but the landscape will be way different.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Sask stop sign white triangles
text: Those white triangles(can be different ammount of them) on signposts of stop signs are unique to Saskatchewan.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Newfoundland bins
text: Bins made of wood planks can be seen on Newfoundland driveways. These are most commonly octagonal, however they can have other shapes.
NOTE: Although they are most common in Newfoundland, they can also sometimes be seen in other provinces, such as New Brunswick.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Newfoundland fire hydrant markers
text: Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Concrete barriers
text: British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Wooden post pyramid top
text: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Ontario traffic cones
text: Ontario uses distinct orange and black striped traffic cones.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Manitoba bollards
text: Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one.
Wooden, rectangular bollards of this form are typically found further north in Manitoba
NOTE: Bollards in this format with just a black top are seen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Transformers facing the road
text: The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: 45° angle transformers
text: Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Saskatchewan white bits
text: Yellow center lines in Saskatchewan frequently have tiny white bits in and around them. You can also rarely find them in BC and Yukon, but the landscape there should be different enough to not get them confused.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Roadlines
text: Canadian roads usually have single yellow centre lines.
However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common.
**NOTE:** Double yellow centre lines are more common in the US. This is not a 100% reliable clue, so make sure to use this along with other clues.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: New Brunswick Arrêt/Stop
text: Stop signs in New Brunswick always have the word "Stop" written in France (Arrêt) in addition to the English word.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Québec Arrêt
text: Stop signs in Québec always have the word "Stop" written in France (Arrêt). Beware that "Arrêt" is also written on New Brunswick stop signs!

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Maximum Speed Sign
text: Canada uses the word ‘maximum’ on speed signs.
The US uses the words ‘speed limit’ on such signs.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Google car: Gen 2
text: Canada has a fair amount of Generation 2 coverage, especially in rural or remote areas.
Generation 2 can be recognized by the big circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.
If you are between Canada and the US, and the location is in Generation 2, you are much more likely to be in Canada.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

Some provinces use different designs.
Canada is the only country in the world where you can find these signs.

clues.title: Vegetation: Cape Breton National Park
text: The Cape Breton Highlands in northeastern Nova Scotia have an unusual amount of elevation for Eastern Canadian standards. It is very forested, with a mix of broad-leaf trees and pine trees.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Drumheller Canyons
text: The area near Drumheller, Alberta has distinct canyon-like treeless rock formations that comprise the landscape.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: South Saskatchewan Hills
text: Southern Saskatchewan has many river valleys, which means that the province can have a barren hilly landscape; much more so than the rest of the Canadian Great Plains, which tends to be really flat.
NOTE: Some of this hilliness extends into southern Alberta and Manitoba.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Max Max North Coverage
text: The northernmost Google Street View coverage in the world is a trekker on Ellesmere Island in northern Nunavut. It shows a glacier in a rocky, desolate landscape that is devoid of any vegetation.

NOTE: This coverage is sometimes used in maps to improve and standardise the scoring range. As a result, you might encounter this trekker in competitive maps like ACW, despite it not being pinpointable.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Southern British Columbia
text: The landscape in the interior of southern British Columbia, mostly centred around the towns of Kamloops and Kelowna, has a distinct look. It is generally hilly and a little more arid than the rest of BC, The vegetation consists of sprawling brown grasslands, and pine tree forests on the hillsides.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Québec City Windsor Corridor
text: The Québec City-Windsor Corridor is the most densely populated part of Canada. It is mostly flat and green, with a patchwork of agriculture and occasional forest cover.
NOTE: This area can look similar to the Great Lakes region in the US.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Western Mountains
text: Western Canada is very mountainous. The highest mountains are in British Columbia, western Alberta, and parts of Yukon. Outside these provinces, large mountains are rare to non-existent in Canada.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Yukon
text: Yukon has a very northern, boreal landscape that is mostly hilly, sometimes with large mountains in the distance. Coniferous trees line the roads and the further north you go, the thinner and shorter the trees get. While this region recently got a lot of new Generation 4, older Generation 2 coverage is still very common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Great Plains
text: The Great Plains are mostly flat, with some rolling hills. There is a lot of agriculture, very few trees, and it is very sparsely populated. The landscape gets drier the further south-southwest you go, with the driest parts near the border with the US state of Montana.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Gaspé Peninsula
text: The inland roads of the Gaspé Peninsula feature densely forested mountainous terrain. It is particularly common to encounter overcast coverage in this region.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
